name: eRPC
baseline: NSDI'19 paper baselines: FaSST RPCs and raw RDMA reads/writes (measured; eRPC is comparable but slightly slower), IX (per-core RPC rate quoted from the IX paper), NetChain and ZabFPGA replication (their published numbers), and the Cell RDMA B-tree (published numbers). The paper never benchmarks kernel TCP/UDP socket RPC or HERD.
workload: Small (32-byte) and large (8MB) RPC calls over Ethernet/InfiniBand/RoCE NICs, plus a 3-way Raft replication port, on commodity DPDK-capable or Mellanox NICs
claimed_speedup: NSDI'19 paper: one core handles ~10M small RPCs/s vs ~1.5M 64 B RPCs/s with IX (IX figure quoted, not re-measured; ~6.7x derived from page data). 3-way Raft replication takes 5.5 us median vs NetChain's published 9.7 us (~1.8x, derived from page data) and is 3% slower than ZabFPGA at the leader (3.1 vs 3.0 us). Masstree-over-eRPC median GET is 2.7 us, 'around 10x faster' than Cell's RDMA B-tree. Against its measured RDMA baselines eRPC is slightly slower: per-thread small-RPC rate up to 18% below FaSST, median latency up to 800 ns above RDMA reads, and at least 70% of RDMA-write bandwidth for requests of 32 kB or more (75 Gbps peak on one core). The README's absolute figures (2.3 us RTT, ~10M RPCs/s per core, 60-80M RPCs/s per NIC, 75 Gbps, 5.3 us Raft) have no baseline on that page. The paper gives 5.5 us, not 5.3 us, for Raft and does not contain the 60-80M per NIC figure.
compiler_and_flags: The paper does not state them. The repo's CMakeLists.txt with the default PERF=ON uses CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE RelWithDebInfo plus -std=c++11 -march=native. The compiler is not named.
hardware: NSDI'19 Table 1 lists three clusters. CX3: 11 nodes, 56 Gbps ConnectX-3 InfiniBand, Intel Xeon E5-2650 (8 cores). CX4: 100 CloudLab nodes, 25 GbE ConnectX-4 Lx lossy Ethernet, Xeon E5-2640 v4 (10 cores). CX5: 8 nodes, dual-port 40 GbE ConnectX-5, Xeon E5-2697 v3 (14 cores) or E5-2683 v4 (16 cores). Large-RPC bandwidth was measured between two CX5 nodes over 100 Gbps ConnectX-5 InfiniBand.
tradeoffs: Requires DPDK/RDMA-capable NICs and huge pages; a binary RPC library, not an HTTP-semantics server (no TLS/HTTP parsing); app must integrate its session/event-loop model
caveats: The paper's thesis is that eRPC is comparable to specialized systems while staying general. It never measures kernel TCP/UDP socket RPC or HERD, and against FaSST and raw RDMA it is slightly slower. Its 'faster' comparisons (IX, NetChain, Cell, and FaRM at scale) use numbers from other papers on different hardware; the authors say the NetChain comparison 'must be taken with a grain of salt'. The category fit is datacenter RPC over DPDK/RDMA rather than HTTP serving. The README's 5.3 us Raft and 60-80M RPCs/s per NIC figures are not in the paper, which gives 5.5 us. Authors now point new users to microsoft/machnet. The LICENSE file is the Apache-2.0 notice header (GitHub reports NOASSERTION).

name: FlexTOE
baseline: Linux host TCP stack, TAS (TCP Acceleration as an OS Service), and the Chelsio Terminator hardware TCP offload engine
workload: Memcached and RPC microbenchmarks on an Agilio-CX40 SmartNIC, plus single-connection RPC throughput on x86 and BlueField hosts
claimed_speedup: From the abstract, arXiv 2110.10919 and NSDI'22 alike: Memcached scales up to 38% better than TAS and saves up to 81% of host CPU cycles vs Chelsio. 99.99th-percentile RPC RTT is 3.2x lower than Chelsio and 50% lower than TAS. Single-connection RPC throughput is up to 2.4x TAS on x86 and 4x TAS on BlueField. The full paper's Linux-kernel-TCP figures: Memcached throughput up to 5.5x Linux, 4.9x Chelsio and 1.6x TAS (Fig. 8). RPC throughput at 250 cycles/RPC is up to 4x Linux and 5.3x Chelsio when receiving, and over 7.6x Linux and Chelsio when sending (Fig. 10). With up to 2K connections it reaches 3.3x Linux. FlexTOE loses in some cases: median small-RPC latency is 20 us vs 14 us for Chelsio and 16 us for TAS, and TAS is 1.5x better in the connection-scalability benchmark.
compiler_and_flags: SmartNIC firmware was built with the NFP compiler toolchain 6.1.0.1. The host compiler and flags are not stated.
hardware: Two 20-core Intel Xeon Gold 6138 @ 2 GHz servers (40 GB RAM), each with a Netronome Agilio CX40 40 Gbps, a Chelsio Terminator T62100-LP-CR 100 Gbps and an Intel XL710 40 Gbps NIC. Extra clients: two 2x18-core Xeon Gold 6154 @ 3 GHz (ConnectX-5 100 Gbps) and two 4-core Xeon E3-1230 v5 @ 3.4 GHz (82599ES 10 Gbps), on a 100 Gbps switch. The generalization runs used a Mellanox BlueField MBF1M332A-ASCAT 25 Gbps SmartNIC and a 32-core AMD EPYC 7452 @ 2.35 GHz host with a ConnectX-5 100 Gbps NIC.
tradeoffs: Requires a Netronome Agilio SmartNIC; programmability via C/eBPF/XDP adds development complexity vs. a plain sockets server; unmaintained since 2022
caveats: FlexTOE needs a Netronome Agilio (NFP-4000/6000) SmartNIC and 1G hugepages; the x86 and BlueField ports are described in the paper's appendix E but no separate port or benchmark directory is visible in the repo tree. It trades median latency for tail latency and throughput (20 us median vs 14-16 us for Chelsio/TAS), and TAS beats it by 1.5x on connection scalability. TAS ran on an Intel XL710 because of a slow Agilio DPDK driver. The category fit is a TCP offload engine rather than an HTTP server. The TAS baseline is an academic stack; the Linux kernel TCP stack is the recognizable incumbent (up to 5.5x Memcached throughput).
found_via: arXiv query 'TAS TCP Acceleration OS Service Kaufmann' -> https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.10919 (FlexTOE: Flexible TCP Offload with Fine-Grained Parallelism)

verification.tier_reason: The peer-reviewed NSDI'22 paper measures FlexTOE head-to-head against the Linux kernel TCP stack, TAS and the Chelsio T6 TOE on the same testbed (Xeon Gold 6138 hosts) and shows wins. name: Lithium (HTTP server / web framework)
baseline: actix-web (best TechEmpower actix implementation in Round 20, actix-core; also actix-pg). H2O is a secondary comparison from the author's own statement.
workload: TechEmpower Framework Benchmarks (TFB) composite-score suite: JSON serialization, plaintext, single/multi-row DB queries, Fortunes template rendering, and DB updates, using non-blocking HTTP I/O and pipelined/batched PostgreSQL queries.
claimed_speedup: TechEmpower Round 20, the official run on Citrine physical hardware, completed 2021-01-04. Best responses/sec per test comes from the results JSON (derived from page data). lithium-postgres-batch vs actix-core: single query 833,811 vs 635,092 (1.31x); 20 queries 59,452 vs 34,956 (1.70x); updates at 20 queries 34,888 vs 24,301 (1.44x); Fortunes 618,610 vs 653,529 (0.95x, slower). JSON is 1,599,157 (lithium-postgres-beta) vs 1,563,587 (actix-raw), 1.02x. Plaintext is about 7.00M for both (network-bound tie). lithium-postgres-batch had the top single-query result of all implementations and was second in 20-query and updates. The earlier HN post (2020-08-29) only says in its title that Lithium 'ranked the highest performance web application platform' in a continuous run's composite view; it gives no rps numbers. On HN the author said non-batched Lithium is 'as fast (slighly faster on some tests, slighly slower on others)' as H2O. One commenter wrote '2x faster than the Actix Rust framework', which is unverified.
compiler_and_flags: TechEmpower Round-20-era build (FrameworkBenchmarks commit 68c13b5c, 2020-11-11): lithium-postgres-batch.dockerfile uses buildpack-deps:focal and apt clang (LLVM 10, called as llvm-profdata-10). compile-batch.sh builds lithium_batch.cc with clang++ -O3 -march=native -flto -std=c++17 -DNDEBUG -DN_SQL_CONNECTIONS=1 and two-pass PGO (-fprofile-instr-generate, then -fprofile-instr-use). It links a patched libpq (compile_libpq.sh batchmode), and the Lithium single headers are pinned at commit 10b72ad8. Baseline actix-core: FROM rust:1.44, RUSTFLAGS="-C target-cpu=native" cargo build --release.
hardware: TechEmpower Citrine (rounds 16-22): three Dell R440 servers (application, database, load generator), each with an Intel Xeon Gold 5120 CPU, 32 GB RAM and an enterprise SSD, on a dedicated Cisco 10-gigabit Ethernet switch. The August 2020 continuous run 57b25c85 also ran on Citrine.
tradeoffs: Async/pipelined Postgres query batching depends on a non-upstream patched fork of libpq (dating to a 2016 patch that was never merged upstream), a dependency risk the author himself flagged and which is shared with drogon; Linux/macOS only (no Windows support); framework is effectively superseded/merged from the author's earlier 'silicon' project.
caveats: The Round 20 win depends on the libpq pipelining/batch variant (lithium-postgres-batch). On 2022-05-31 TechEmpower removed these tests (PR #7382) 'to comply with the benchmark rules'. In later official data Lithium is slower than actix on database tests. Round 21 vs actix-http: single query 377,722 vs 512,831 (0.74x); 20 queries 0.66x; Fortunes 0.75x; updates 0.73x. Round 22: 0.82x, 0.80x, 0.86x and 0.91x on the same tests (derived from page data). In Rounds 22-23 Lithium is also below H2O on all database tests. It is only equal to or slightly above actix on JSON and plaintext. Brian from TechEmpower cautioned on HN that the August 2020 continuous run (57b25c85, TFB commit 4a00589b) had not received official-round sanity checking and 'should be taken with a grain of salt'. That run's results data is not archived: tfb-status.techempower.com is unreachable, and Wayback holds only the status page, not results.json. The HN thread's remark about actix is from commenter The_rationalist, not the author, and says the opposite of the earlier record: actix-web DID benefit from query pipelining because tokio-postgres is its own implementation and does not use libpq. The README still says Lithium is 'ranked #1 on the TechEmpower benchmark (composite score)'; this is out of date. TechEmpower/FrameworkBenchmarks was archived on 2026-03-24. Linux-only (epoll).
found_via: HN Algolia search 'lithium techempower' -> story https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=24315285 (posted by matt42, the project author); cross-checked against https://github.com/matt-42/lithium README claim 'ranked #1 on the TechEmpower benchmark (composite score)'.

verification.tier_reason: Upgraded from B. The HN page has no numbers, so benchmark_url now points to the official TechEmpower Round 20 physical-environment results JSON. That file has per-test totals for lithium-postgres-batch, actix-core and actix-pg, all run on Citrine hardware (Intel Xeon Gold 5120). The benchmark code is public in TechEmpower/FrameworkBenchmarks: frameworks/C++/lithium/lithium_batch.cc and compile-batch.sh, plus frameworks/Rust/actix/actix-core.dockerfile. At Round-20-era commit 68c13b5c, the build files state clang from buildpack-deps:focal (LLVM 10, called as llvm-profdata-10) with -O3 -march=native -flto -std=c++17 plus two-pass PGO. The actix build states rust:1.44 with RUSTFLAGS="-C target-cpu=native" cargo build --release.
verification.notes: Metadata confirmed via gh GraphQL, because REST returned a 403 rate limit: MIT license, not a fork, not archived, 1,409 stars, last commit 2026-07-31 (active). Round 20 per-test numbers are best rps per implementation computed from the rawData totalRequests over the 15 s runs. The composite score could not be recomputed because TechEmpower sets per-round weights that are not published in the JSON. The entry is a real, notable win against actix-web, but only in 2020 to early 2021, with the pipelined database variant, and it did not last. Consider tagging it as a historical result.

name: Shenango
baseline: ZygOS (a state-of-the-art kernel-bypass network stack) and standard Linux kernel networking
workload: memcached 1.5.6 USR workload (99.8% GET / 0.2% SET) over TCP; Rust spin-server with constant/exponential/bimodal service times (10 us mean); gdnsd 2.4.0 DNS over UDP. Each runs alongside PARSEC swaptions batch work, with 1,200 persistent connections from 6 client machines and all systems limited to 16 hyperthreads. Also load-burst tests (100k to 5M requests/s) and thread-operation microbenchmarks vs pthreads, Go and Arachne. Core reallocation every 5 us.
claimed_speedup: NSDI'19 paper: memcached (USR workload): Shenango handles over 5 million requests/s with 37 us median and 93 us 99.9th-percentile latency, keeping 99.9th-percentile latency below 100 us at 'one million more than ZygOS' (ZygOS keeps similar response times only up to ~4 million requests/s). Linux memcached reaches about 800,000 requests/s before 99th-percentile latency spikes (no batch work). With batch work, Linux's 99.9th-percentile latency at 0.4M requests/s goes from 83 us to over 2 ms. gdnsd DNS over UDP: Linux up to 900,000 requests/s (41 us median) vs Shenango 5.7 million requests/s, 'a 6.33x improvement' (36 us median, 73 us 99.9th percentile). Thread microbenchmarks (Table 2): spawn-join 148 ns vs 12,996 ns with Linux pthreads; condvar ping-pong 100 ns vs 1,900 ns. Per the abstract, unlike ZygOS, Shenango can linearly trade latency-sensitive throughput for batch-processing throughput.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the paper. Repo Makefiles: gcc (runtime/IOKernel) and g++ (apps/bench) with -O3 -DNDEBUG -mssse3 (non-DEBUG build); Rust apps built with cargo --release on nightly. No compiler versions given.
hardware: Dual-socket server with 12-core Intel Xeon E5-2650v4 @ 2.20 GHz (first socket only, hyper-threads on, TurboBoost, C-states and frequency scaling disabled), 64 GB RAM, 10 Gb/s Intel 82599ES NIC; Ubuntu 18.04, kernel 4.15.0 (ZygOS on Ubuntu 16.04, kernel 4.11.0); load from six quad-core machines through a Mellanox SX1024 switch with ConnectX-3 Pro NICs
tradeoffs: Requires DPDK and a dedicated IOKernel scheduling process; kernel-bypass core reallocation adds operational complexity
caveats: The README says 'This repository is no longer maintained' and points to the successor shenango/caladan. The last commit (2024-11-05) only adds that README notice, so the entry stays marked abandoned. By commit age alone (about 23 months) the rule would give 'stale'. The benchmark_url abstract page has only the qualitative claim; the numbers are in the paper PDF. ZygOS reaches higher peak memcached throughput than Shenango, but at a high latency cost. At memcached's very short service times (<2 us) the IOKernel becomes the bottleneck. Shenango dedicates a full core (2 hyperthreads) to the IOKernel. The main win is CPU efficiency (batch throughput recovered) at equal tail latency, not raw speed over kernel-bypass stacks. The successor Caladan (shenango/caladan, Apache-2.0, 200 stars, pushed 2026-09-25) was published at OSDI'20, not NSDI'20: https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi20/presentation/fried. Its abstract claims an 11,000x tail-latency reduction vs Parties (580 ms to 52 us).

name: aeronet
workload: wrk-driven HTTP/1.1 benchmark (1 thread, 30s duration, 5s warmup) across headers/body/body-codec/static/cpu/mixed/files/routing scenarios at 10 and 100 connections, run in CI against scripted competitor servers built from the same harness.
claimed_speedup: vs beast (10 conns): headers 12,035.73 vs 4,376.77 req/s (2.75x), static 54,259.34 vs 49,281.00 (1.10x), routing 57,644.49 vs 47,995.38 (1.20x). vs go net/http (10 conns): headers 12,035.73 vs 3,996.83 (3.0x), static 54,259.34 vs 25,399.27 (2.14x), routing 57,644.49 vs 28,141.20 (2.05x), mixed 25,261.40 vs 9,003.95 (2.81x), body 3,827.02 vs 407.32 (9.4x); at 100 conns aeronet leads go net/http in every scenario (e.g. static 93,479.14 vs 37,787.70, routing 91,957.05 vs 44,446.00) (all derived from page data)

name: Demikernel
workload: SOSP'21: 64 B echo server/client (1M echos, 5 runs); UDP relay (TURN) server driven by a Linux traffic generator; Redis via redis-benchmark GET/SET (64 B values, 1M keys, in-memory and with a per-SET fsync append-only log); TxnStore under YCSB-t. Compared against Linux POSIX sockets/epoll, io_uring and kernel-bypass systems (eRPC, Shenango, Caladan, DPDK testpmd, RDMA perftest). The 2019 blog ran the Redis benchmark on CloudLab.
claimed_speedup: SOSP'21 paper, 64 B echo RTT on Linux hosts (Fig. 5): Linux POSIX 30.4 us vs Catnip (DPDK) UDP 6.0 us + 0.025 us of Demikernel time, Catnip TCP 7.1 + 0.053 us, Catmint (RDMA) 5.3 + 0.949 us. That is about 4.3-5x lower RTT with Catnip (derived from page data). UDP relay server (Fig. 10): average 24.9 us on Linux vs 13.9 us on Catnip, p99 27.6 vs 14.9 us; the paper says 'Catnip reduces the server-side latency per request by 11us on average and 13.7us at the p99' (io_uring: 24.4/25.8 us). Redis in-memory peak throughput vs unmodified Redis on Linux (Fig. 11): 'Catmint gives 2x throughput, and Catnip offers 20% better throughput'. Azure VM: 'Catnip offers a 5x latency improvement over the Linux kernel'. The 2019 first-party blog (CloudLab Redis) says '60% of the latency comes from the OS kernel and its interface' (30% from interface inefficiency, another 30% removed by RDMA/DPDK kernel bypass).
hardware: SOSP'21 Linux cluster: 5 servers with 20-core dual-socket Intel Xeon Silver 4114 @ 2.2 GHz, Mellanox CX-5 100 Gbps NICs, Arista 7060CX 100 Gbps switch, Intel Optane 800P NVMe. Windows cluster: 14-core dual-socket Xeon 2690 @ 2.6 GHz with Mellanox CX-4 56 Gbps. The 2019 blog used CloudLab with a 25Gb network and Mellanox CX-4 NICs.
tradeoffs: Project explicitly labeled a research prototype with 'no guarantees'; requires DPDK/RDMA hardware for the kernel-bypass LibOSes (catnip); Linux-socket LibOS (catnap) has no bypass benefit by itself
caveats: The SOSP'21 paper is open access at the first author's site; the ACM DL PDF returned HTTP 403 to automated fetches, but the paper is not paywalled. The wins are against the Linux kernel sockets/epoll path. Against other kernel-bypass stacks Demikernel is competitive rather than uniformly faster: Catnip echo is 1.7 us slower than Caladan, Catnip (UDP) reaches 70% of Caladan's peak throughput, and Catmint reaches 46% of eRPC's. The Linux-sockets LibOS (Catnap) busy-polls a full core and has lower Redis peak throughput than unmodified Redis. The gains need DPDK/RDMA-capable NICs, and the README calls the project a prototype with no guarantees. The paper states no Rust/compiler version or build flags.

name: Drogon
workload:

Hello, world!

' from an HttpSimpleController on /benchmark, 16 Drogon threads) versus an nginx module returning the same body, load generated with httpress at 100/1000/10000 connections with and without keep-alive; each setting run five times, max and min recorded.

BenchmarkCtrl calls resp->setExpiredTime(0), so Drogon serves a framework-cached, pre-rendered response; the current examples/benchmark/main.cc no longer matches the wiki setup (it registers a sync advice on '/' and uses setThreadNum(0)). Nginx is run through a hand-written module rather than serving a static file, which is not the usual nginx deployment. The no-keep-alive 100-connection row was run with httpress -t 12 while the other rows used -t 16, and its nginx figure is inconsistent (31/49, max below min). name: Qbix Server (PHP webserver)
workload: PHP request handling with a simulated 50ms I/O wait (usleep), c=40, measured with ab. php-fpm is held to 4 persistent workers on the assumption of 4 x 50MB = 200MB; Qbix octane runs COW-forked persistent workers in the same 200MB budget (40 per the table, 100 per the summary/README). Single-core container, PHP 8.3.6, Ubuntu 24.
claimed_speedup: 1,060 req/s (Qbix octane persistent workers) vs 78 req/s (php-fpm, 4 workers) under 50ms simulated I/O, c=40, same 200MB budget = ~13.6x (derived from page data; doc states '14x'). The worker count behind 1,060 is inconsistent: the BENCHMARKS.md table says 40 workers, but the same doc's summary and the README say 100 workers.
hardware: single-core container, Ubuntu 24, PHP 8.3.6; no CPU model stated
tradeoffs: Relies on pcntl_fork() (Unix/Linux only, no Windows); the memory/worker-count advantage under I/O-bound load is the whole story, not raw per-request latency; on CPU-bound work it loses to Swoole (439 vs 483 req/s) and roughly ties php-fpm.
caveats: The worker count is internally inconsistent. The table says 40 workers reached 1,060 req/s at 50ms I/O, but 40 workers x 20 req/s is a theoretical ceiling of 800 req/s, by the doc's own '4 workers x 20 req/s = 80' math. The summary and README say 100 workers. The fpm side is capped at 4 workers by an assumed 50MB/worker budget; fpm was not measured running out of memory, and the doc elsewhere gives ~42MB/worker, or ~24 workers/GB. The same page's c=200 test shows a smaller gain at 50ms I/O: 358 vs 79 req/s (4.5x), with 200 octane workers. On CPU-bound work fpm beats octane (469 vs 439, 3,940 vs 2,609 and 5,048 vs 2,818 req/s). On static files nginx beats Qbix (50,742 vs 18,311 req/s). The repo description's 'Handle over 100x more traffic' refers to worker density, not measured throughput; the best measured throughput gain is ~14x. The I/O is simulated with usleep. No CPU model is stated.

name: uhttp (io_uring-http-benchmark)
workload: Serving a single 10,240-byte static HTML file over loopback on 2 physical cores; wrk from 6 separate client cores, 45s runs x3 repetitions, interleaved targets, at 64/256/1024/4096 connections, plus perf-measured instructions/cycles/IPC per request.
claimed_speedup: 40-54% more requests/sec than tuned nginx at the same connection counts (64 conns: 358,428 vs 256,046 req/s = +40%; 1024 conns: 315,095 vs 204,644 = +54%; 4096 conns: 276,195 vs 184,395 = +50%); 28-34% less CPU per request (5.8-7.5us vs nginx's 8.1-11.1us); half the instructions per request (17,583 vs 35,831) (verbatim from README table)
compiler_and_flags: CMake Release (Ninja) with explicit Release flags from CMakeLists.txt: -O3 -march=native -fno-plt -fno-semantic-interposition, plus LTO (INTERPROCEDURAL_OPTIMIZATION_RELEASE when supported); needs liburing >= 2.5 and a C++20 compiler; compiler name/version not stated
hardware: Unspecified 'mobile CPU' with SMT (physical cores 0,2,...,14 per bench/run_bench.py, i.e. 8 physical cores); server on 2 physical cores (0,2), wrk on 6 client cores (4-14); exact CPU model not stated; kernel built with CONFIG_INIT_ON_ALLOC_DEFAULT_ON=y; loopback only
tradeoffs: Serves exactly one static route from memory (not general-purpose like nginx); no TLS/HTTP2/CGI; loopback-only benchmark so sendfile's zero-copy advantage on real NICs was not tested; author explicitly documents nginx wins the p99 latency tail at low connection counts and that per-feature attribution of the io_uring gains is unresolved.
caveats: No LICENSE file in the repo (GitHub license API returns 404), so usability=reference despite public code. Exact CPU model and compiler are not stated (only 'mobile CPU'), so this is capped at Tier C even though methodology (warmup, 45 s x3 repetitions, interleaving, client-saturation checks, perf counters) is unusually rigorous for a first-party repo. Loopback only: the author says not to read it as 'io_uring beats sendfile on a real network'. uhttp serves one route from memory while nginx is a general-purpose server, and the author says some of the 2x instruction gap comes from that generality. nginx wins p99 latency at 64 connections (333 us vs 360 us). -march=native build. Per-feature attribution is inside the 3.4% noise floor; send_zc loses 6.6% at this payload size.

name: ChaChaCha
baseline: OpenSSL ChaCha20/ChaCha20-Poly1305 (assembly and EVP), BoringSSL stitched AVX2 ChaCha20-Poly1305
workload: ChaCha20 and ChaCha20-Poly1305 AEAD seal/open at protocol-realistic sizes (QUIC 1200-1350B, WireGuard 1360-1420B, 4KB TLS record, 9000B jumbo, 16384B TLS 1.3 max record, 32-64KiB bulk) measured in core cycles/byte via perf_event_open, pinned to one core, best-of-7 internal reps x best-of-3 runs, on AMD EPYC 9655 (Zen 5) and AMD EPYC 4244P (Zen 4)
claimed_speedup: Page percentages are cycles/byte reductions, (theirs - ours)/theirs, not throughput ratios. Zen 5 AEAD real-world bands vs OpenSSL (vendored asm, called without EVP): seal +19.3% to +45.4% (WireGuard 1360-1420B +45.4%, i.e. 1.83x throughput derived from page data; 16384B +22.4%); open +20.9% to +47.6%. Zen 5 vs BoringSSL stitched AVX2: seal +49.4% to +57.1%, open +53.5% to +57.4%. Zen 5 vs Intel IPsec-MB (best of its two entry points): seal +3.8% to +16.8%, open +4.7% to +19.9%. Zen 4 AEAD vs OpenSSL: seal +8.9% to +33.0%, open +9.2% to +32.5%; vs BoringSSL +30.8% to +37.5%; vs Intel -1.3% to +8.9% (loses at Jumbo 8900-9000B). Raw AVX-512 ChaCha20: +25.0% to +33.1% vs the best other implementation (Intel) on Zen 5 for bands of 4KB and above (vs OpenSSL 16x about +29% to +35%, derived from page data); Zen 4 +5.0% to +7.6% vs best other (vs OpenSSL about +8% to +15%, derived from page data); ours loses to Intel at QUIC/WireGuard sizes (-7.5%/-3.9% Zen 5, -26.0%/-16.5% Zen 4). Raw AVX2 ChaCha20 vs best other (OpenSSL/BoringSSL): +10.0% to +10.8% on Zen 5 and +5.4% to +8.1% on Zen 4 for bands of 4KB and above; about 0% at 1200-1420B.
compiler_and_flags: gcc (version not stated; README requires Linux x86-64 with gcc and make), Makefile CFLAGS ?= -O2 -Wall for C harness/glue, ASFLAGS=-Wa,--noexecstack; kernels are perlasm-generated assembly assembled by gcc plus NASM (-f elf64) for poly1305_ifma.asm and the Intel vendor kernels
hardware: AMD EPYC 9655 (Zen 5, Turin) and AMD EPYC 4244P (Zen 4)
tradeoffs: x86-64 AVX2/AVX-512 only (no portable/scalar-only fallback path shown as competitive); OpenSSL is measured both as raw vendored assembly (openssl-asm) and via EVP (openssl-evp) which carries provider dispatch overhead, so the EVP-vs-EVP comparison would show an even larger margin than the asm-vs-asm numbers quoted; BoringSSL comparison for AVX-512 is AEAD-only since BoringSSL has no AVX-512 ChaCha20 raw kernel; single author, very new/unreviewed project
caveats: Single-author project with 1 GitHub star and no independent reproduction. Only two AMD CPUs tested (Zen 5 EPYC 9655, Zen 4 EPYC 4244P); no Intel CPU results. The AEAD 'OpenSSL' column is OpenSSL's vendored assembly called directly (no stitched AEAD in OpenSSL); OpenSSL EVP has higher fixed per-call cost (1419/1773 cycles vs 650/550 for asm). Ours is slower than OpenSSL asm on small messages (Zen 5 seal 64-256B: -19.6% to -24.0%; Zen 4 seal 64-256B: -9.5% to -23.4%) and roughly equal at exactly 1024B. Page flags power-of-two lengths (1024/2048/4096...) as flattering batch boundaries and uses realistic protocol-size bands for headline tables. Page GB/s figures assume a nominal 3.0 GHz; c/B is the real metric. Methodology is careful: perf_event_open core cycles, pinned core, alternating order, best of 7 x best of 3, round-trip correctness check before timing.

name: curve25519 (mehdi sotoodeh / "Mehdi")
baseline: OpenSSL 1.1.1 EVP_PKEY API: EVP_PKEY_ED25519 (CreateKeyPair, SignMessage via EVP_DigestSign) and EVP_PKEY_X25519 (CalculatePublicKey, CreateSharedKey via EVP_PKEY_derive)
workload: test/openssl_test.c: Ed25519 key-pair creation, X25519 public-key derivation, X25519 shared-secret computation and Ed25519 signing of a 32-byte message; min of 100 runs per operation timed with rdtsc (TSC ticks, minus rdtsc overhead), comparing the x86-64 assembly library build ('make asm && make openssl') against OpenSSL's EVP_PKEY API; outputs are memcmp-checked for equality
claimed_speedup: README OpenSSL comparison (HP EliteBook 755 G5, Ubuntu 18.04.2, OpenSSL 1.1.1; TSC cycles, the '@3.4GHz' usec figures are a fixed constant in the test code): CreateKeyPair 74,822 vs 210,738 cycles (ratio 2.817, delta 64.50%); CalculatePublicKey 316,096 vs 208,714 (ratio 0.660, Mehdi 51.45% slower); CreateSharedKey 270,930 vs 442,750 (ratio 1.634, delta 38.81%); SignMessage 78,628 vs 425,656 (ratio 5.414, delta 81.53%). The OpenSSL timed region also includes EVP_PKEY creation from the raw secret (plus peer-key and context setup for CreateSharedKey), while the Mehdi SignMessage call receives a precomputed 64-byte private+public key, so the CreateSharedKey and SignMessage margins are not like-for-like. Separately, X25519 base-point multiplication is 5.33x to 19.59x faster than curve25519-donna across the README platform/compiler table (README text says 6.2 to 19.5); fastest 43,229 cycles (W7-64/MASM V1.1, Intel Core i7-2670QM).
compiler_and_flags: gcc via Rules.mk (version not stated for the OpenSSL run); source/asm64/Makefile compiles the C glue with -O2 -m64 -Wall -Wno-format -DUSE_ASM_LIB and assembles amd64.gnu/*.s with 'as --64'; test objects, including openssl_test.c, use -O2; RELEASE=1 adds -DNDEBUG, otherwise -g -D_DEBUG. The portable-C library (source/Makefile) also uses -O2. Donna table: VS2010/MASM, GNU assembler 2.25 (mingw) and gcc 4.5.3 (Cygwin-32).
hardware: OpenSSL comparison: HP EliteBook 755 G5 laptop, x86_64 (CPU model not stated), Ubuntu 18.04.2; donna comparison and internal cycle tables: Intel Core i7-2670QM
tradeoffs: One of four benchmarked operations (CalculatePublicKey) is markedly slower than OpenSSL, so the library is not a strict win across the board; portable-C build has no stated optimization level (only the asm build is used for the OpenSSL comparison); constant-time/blinding variants are slower than the non-hardened V1.1 numbers; abandoned since 2020, predates OpenSSL 3.x and modern OpenSSL X25519/Ed25519 assembly optimizations, so the OpenSSL side of the comparison is likely stale
caveats: OpenSSL comparison dates from June 2019 (commit 'Performance comparison with OpenSSL') against OpenSSL 1.1.1 on one laptop whose CPU model is not given. OpenSSL-side timings include EVP_PKEY object creation from the raw secret inside the timed loop, and the Mehdi SignMessage side gets a precomputed public key, so the SignMessage and CreateSharedKey margins are inflated; the like-for-like CalculatePublicKey (X25519) row shows this library 51.45% slower than OpenSSL. Minimum of 100 TSC-timed runs, not core cycles. Current OpenSSL 3.x results are unknown. The curve25519-donna comparison (5.33x-19.59x) uses a different, non-list baseline across different compilers/platforms. Repo has had no commits since 2020-04-20.

name: EverCrypt (HACL*) Curve25519 (Vale-optimized)
workload: Curve25519 scalar multiplication (the X25519 ECDH used in TLS 1.3), average CPU cycles per operation. The other implementations were measured in-kernel with Donenfeld's kbench9000 cycle counter. OpenSSL was measured 'using the same script, but in user space', because it cannot be called from the kernel.
claimed_speedup: EverCrypt's targeted Curve25519 (Low* C plus Vale Intel ADX asm) takes 113,614 CPU cycles per scalar multiplication. OpenSSL's ADX asm takes 118,604. That is about 4.2% fewer cycles, or about 1.04x (derived from page data, Figure 9 of 'EverCrypt: A Fast, Verified, Cross-Platform Cryptographic Provider', IEEE S&P 2020). The paper's text says EverCrypt beats Oliveira et al. (115,122 cycles) by about 1%, and that Oliveira et al. 'in turn exceeds that of OpenSSL by 3%'. It also says EverCrypt beats Erbsen et al./fiat-crypto (145,248 cycles) by 22%.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 7.3, -O3 -march=native -mtune=native
hardware: Intel Kaby Lake i7-7560 (the paper's wording; the record's i7-7560U suffix is not in the paper)
stars_or_usage: 1,837 stars. hacl-star.github.io says code from HACL*, ValeCrypt and EverCrypt is deployed in Mozilla Firefox's NSS, the Linux kernel, mbedTLS, the Tezos blockchain, the ElectionGuard SDK and the WireGuard VPN.
tradeoffs: Source is written in F*/Low*/Vale and compiled via KaRaMeL to C/assembly rather than hand-written C; gains formal proofs of memory safety, functional correctness and secret-independence (constant-time) at the cost of a heavy build toolchain (F*, KaRaMeL, Vale) compared to a plain C/asm library.
caveats: The gain over OpenSSL is only about 4% in cycles (derived). The record's '~3% over OpenSSL' misreads the paper: that 3% is Oliveira et al. over OpenSSL. The result is from one 2017-era Kaby Lake CPU, against an OpenSSL build from 2018-19 (commit e8fb288). OpenSSL ran in user space while the other implementations ran in-kernel via kbench9000, so the environments differ. The public kbench9000 kb/x25519 branch holds the EverCrypt/Vale code and the other contenders but no OpenSSL harness, so the OpenSSL comparison cannot be fully reproduced from public code. The paper's AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305 figures (Figures 7-8, i9-9900K) say only that EverCrypt 'meets or exceeds' OpenSSL, so do not extrapolate to other primitives. The README calls hacl-star the research home and points production users to https://github.com/cryspen/hacl-packages. The repo is Apache-2.0, and the generated C code is also MIT.

name: rustls
workload: Single-core in-process TLS benchmark, rustls 0.23.37 (aws-lc-rs 1.16.0 provider) vs OpenSSL 3.6.1 and BoringSSL 30cd935: bulk transfer (TLS 1.2 AES-128-GCM, TLS 1.3 AES-256-GCM) send/receive MB/s, full handshakes (RSA and ECDSA, TLS 1.2/1.3, client and server) and resumed handshakes per second. Earlier 2023 run (aochagavia/rustls-bench-results, rustls 0.22.0 vs OpenSSL 3.2.0) adds ChaCha20 throughput and per-session memory.
claimed_speedup: 2026-03-07 report, rustls 0.23.37 vs OpenSSL 3.6.1: rustls is faster on every reported row. Full handshakes 1.32x-2.59x, e.g. TLS 1.2 RSA client 8,122.99 vs 3,186.87/s (2.55x), TLS 1.2 RSA server 2,835.45 vs 2,154.41/s (1.32x), TLS 1.2 ECDSA server 13,524.99 vs 5,226.96/s (2.59x), TLS 1.3 RSA server 2,357.36 vs 1,712.64/s (1.38x). Resumed handshakes 1.87x-3.20x (TLS 1.2 server 72,480.52 vs 22,647.1/s). Bulk transfer 1.11x-1.27x (TLS 1.2 AES-128-GCM receive 7,946.96 vs 7,129.43 MB/s; TLS 1.3 AES-256-GCM send 7,421.02 vs 5,844.35 MB/s). Ratios derived from page data. The older 2023 run (rustls 0.22.0 vs OpenSSL 3.2.0) was mixed: client full handshakes 1.93x (TLS 1.2, 4,991.73 vs 2,581.16/s) and 2.06x (TLS 1.3), resumed handshakes 1.56x-3.30x, but server full RSA handshakes 0.70x/0.73x, receive throughput 0.83x-0.93x, ChaCha20-Poly1305 0.56x-0.58x; peak memory 131,816 KiB vs 688,436 KiB for 10,000 TLS 1.3 sessions (-81%).
compiler_and_flags: 2026 report: GCC 12.2.0 and Clang 14.0.6, Rust 1.94.0. OpenSSL 3.6.1 built with default './Configure ; make -j12'; BoringSSL with 'CC=clang CXX=clang++ cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release'; rustls-bench run from target/release via admin/bench-measure.mk; openssl-bench harness 82b86b22 built from its makefile. 2023 run: same C/C++ toolchains, rustls built with 'cargo build -p rustls --release --example bench' (aws_lc_rs feature), jemalloc, openssl-bench harness CXXFLAGS -O2.
hardware: Intel Xeon E-2386G (AVX-512), 32GB, Debian 12 (Bookworm), bare metal, hyper-threading and dynamic frequency scaling disabled, performance governor
stars_or_usage: 7.6k stars; used in curl, AWS, Cloudflare and other production TLS stacks
tradeoffs: Mixed results depending on cipher/direction: faster handshakes, resumption, and far lower memory use, but slower AES128-GCM receive throughput and notably slower ChaCha20-Poly1305 throughput than OpenSSL on this hardware; numbers are tied to the aws-lc crypto backend chosen for rustls, not rustls's own crypto code.
caveats: First-party numbers (rustls maintainers' own rustls.dev/perf reports) but fully pinned and reproducible. Single-core, single-machine benchmarks; ChaCha20 is absent from the 2026 table and was 0.56x-0.58x of OpenSSL in the 2023 run (OpenSSL AVX-512 path). rustls uses aws-lc-rs (AWS-LC) as its crypto provider, so primitive speed is largely AWS-LC's. BoringSSL still beats rustls on bulk send in the 2026 table (8,291.9 vs 8,133.85 MB/s TLS 1.2 AES-128-GCM). rustls is itself one of the three named baselines for this category (OpenSSL, BoringSSL, rustls), so this entry records rustls vs OpenSSL, not a project beating rustls. The original record's 2023 figures come from the aochagavia/rustls-bench-results README itself (not a bencher.dev summary), and its '131.8MB vs 688.4MB' is really 131,816 KiB vs 688,436 KiB.

name: ztls
workload: Sans-I/O TLS 1.3 in-memory application-data round trips (client-to-server, server-to-client, ping-pong) at record sizes 16B, 128B, 1350B, 8192B, 16384B, across TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384, and TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256, over caller-owned in-memory transport (no sockets), n=10 captures with formal confidence intervals
claimed_speedup: Headline row (AppPingPong AES-128-GCM 1350B, x86_64 c7i.2xlarge, n=10): ztls 790.7 ns/op vs rustls 1447.5 ns/op (1.83x) vs OpenSSL libssl 1820.5 ns/op (2.30x). ztls executes 42.7% of libssl's cycles/op and 54.8% of rustls's on that row (row-perf capture). Faster than libssl on all 45 comparable app-data rows on x86_64, aarch64 and macOS (from +4% on ChaCha20 16384B ping-pong on aarch64 to +261% on AES-128-GCM 16B client-to-server on x86_64). Faster than rustls on all 30 AES-GCM rows per platform (x86_64 +65% to +131%). On x86_64 it loses to rustls on ChaCha20-Poly1305 at 16B/128B (-50% to -56%) and, per the benchstat file, by about 6% at 1350B (the page calls this an approximate tie).
compiler_and_flags: Zig 0.15.2, -Doptimize=ReleaseFast, native CPU target, crypto_backend=openssl (OpenSSL 3.6.3 libcrypto via nix); comparison backends OpenSSL 3.6.3 libssl and rustls 0.23.40 (x86_64) / 0.23.41 (aarch64, macOS) release profile, rustc 1.97.0 on the x86_64 capture; benchstat over --count 10 --benchtime 500ms. Captured at git revisions 2c102a5 (x86_64), e39f5a6 (aarch64) and 80083f5 (macOS), before ztls required Zig 0.16
hardware: AWS c7i.2xlarge (Intel Xeon Platinum 8488C, x86_64, KVM guest); AWS c7g.2xlarge, which the page and README call Graviton4 but whose committed lscpu metadata shows Neoverse-V1 / 'AWS Graviton3 CPU @ 2.6GHz'; Apple M1 Max (macOS Darwin 24.6)
tradeoffs: Pre-alpha, API not stable; TLS 1.3 only (no 1.2 fallback, no DTLS, no Windows); crypto primitives (AEAD, ECDHE, signatures, SHA-2) are still delegated to a libcrypto backend (OpenSSL, AWS-LC, or BoringSSL) which allocates during setup, so the zero-allocation claim covers only ztls's own framing/parsing/transcript code, not the crypto backend; loses to rustls on small ChaCha20-Poly1305 records on x86_64; full-handshake row is explicitly documented as non-equivalent across implementations (different certificate-verification scope) and the project itself says not to quote it as a comparison
caveats: Pre-alpha single-author project (7 stars) with no independent reproduction. ztls delegates AEAD, key exchange and SHA-2 to a libcrypto backend (OpenSSL 3.6.3 in all headline captures), the same library as the libssl baseline, so the win over libssl is TLS record-layer and wrapper overhead (WPACKET, tls13_cipher, BIO copies), not faster crypto. Only application-data rows over in-memory transport are compared; the handshake row is explicitly non-equivalent and not claimed. libssl gets one warm-up round while ztls and rustls do not. The captures used Zig 0.15.2 at older revisions, and current ztls requires Zig 0.16. The page labels the c7g.2xlarge host Graviton4, but its lscpu metadata says Graviton3 (Neoverse-V1).
found_via: GitHub: gh search code "handshakes per second" "faster" surfaced mattrobenolt/ztls README and docs/research/PERFORMANCE.md and PRODUCTION_READINESS.md, opened directly

name: AWS-LC
workload: HAProxy 3.1-dev1 (2024-06-26) server-only full TLS handshake (RSA, one HTTP request per new connection, no resumption) and end-to-end TLS session resumption from tickets on both the client and backend sides (10 daisy-chained proxy instances), connections/sec vs thread count up to 64, with pthread rwlocks and with HAProxy's lightweight locks (USE_PTHREAD_EMULATION); the TLS protocol version is not stated
claimed_speedup: HAProxy 3.1-dev1 on a 64-core Graviton4, at 64 threads (bar charts on page). Full TLS handshake (RSA, new conn/s): AWS-LC v1.32.0+30 commits 63.1k (same with or without the C11 build) vs OpenSSL 1.1.1w 48.3k, OpenSSL 3.1.6-3.4.0-dev 42.6-43.2k, OpenSSL 3.0.2/3.0.14 21.2-21.3k (~1.31x vs 1.1.1w, ~1.46-1.48x vs 3.1+, ~3.0x vs 3.0.x; derived from page data). The older AWS-LC 1.29.0 reached only 45.2k (45.7k with -DCMAKE_C_STANDARD=11), below OpenSSL 1.1.1w, because of a CPU-detection bug. TLS resumption (end-to-end conn/s): AWS-LC 1.29.0 built with -DCMAKE_C_STANDARD=11 186.3k (text: ~183k; v1.32+30-c11 183.7k) with either lock type, vs OpenSSL 1.1.1w 17.8k (pthread locks) / 124.1k (HAProxy locks), OpenSSL 3.1-3.4-dev 23.1-27.9k, OpenSSL 3.0.14 3.7k / 8.1k, OpenSSL 3.0.2 1.6k / 2.3k. The page text says '~20% higher than WolfSSL and 50% higher than OpenSSL 1.1.1w'. The default C99 AWS-LC builds (1.29.0 and 1.32+30) collapsed to 8.4-8.5k with pthread locks and 38.4k with HAProxy locks.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 11.4 (stated on page); AWS-LC's CMake config forced C99 (pthread-rwlock refcounting) unless -DCMAKE_C_STANDARD=11 was set; HAProxy built with and without USE_PTHREAD_EMULATION=1; optimization flags not stated
hardware: AWS r8g.16xlarge instance, 64 Graviton4 (ARM Neoverse V2) cores
license: Apache-2.0 OR ISC for new AWS-LC code; the LICENSE file lists BoringSSL-derived code as ISC/Apache-2.0, OpenSSL-derived code as Apache-2.0, and bundled parts as MIT, BSD-3-Clause and CC0 (GitHub reports NOASSERTION)

The ~63k full-handshake figure is for AWS-LC v1.32.0 plus 30 commits, not 1.29.0; 1.29.0 (~45k) trailed OpenSSL 1.1.1w in that test. Only one ARM platform (Graviton4) was tested; gcc 11.4 is stated but optimization flags and the test scripts are not published. Small CC0 parts carry no patent grant.

name: Graviola
workload: One process per run: decode 3 PEM files, then a full TLS 1.3 handshake over loopback TCP (server in main thread, client in another thread), then exit with no application data. wtx TLS stack with a swappable crypto backend (aws-lc-rs, Graviola, ring, OpenSSL via openssl-sys). 5 certificate signature algorithms x 3 key agreements (secp256r1, secp384r1, x25519) x 3 cipher suites. Timed with hyperfine -N, 10 runs after 10 warmups; mean plotted.
claimed_speedup: Page text: "OpenSSL is the slower library" and "Graviola is a promising new cryptography library". Numbers exist only as bar charts (hyperfine mean wall time per process, seconds, 0-0.010 s axis), not box plots. From the SVG bar heights (derived from page data): Graviola about 1.26-5.90 ms vs OpenSSL about 4.41-10.20 ms per full handshake process, about 1.6-3.8x; OpenSSL is slowest in all 45 combinations; Graviola is fastest in only 16 of 45 (ring or aws-lc-rs tie or win the rest).
compiler_and_flags: rustc version not stated (bench Cargo.toml: edition 2024, rust-version = 1.96, wtx 0.49 with 'nightly' feature); cargo profile 'deploy': opt-level=3, lto=true, codegen-units=1, panic=abort, debug-assertions and overflow-checks off (from wtx-bench.tar.xz). OpenSSL version and build flags not stated.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5900X 12-Core, 32GB DDR4, Corsair Force MP510 SSD, Linux Fedora kernel 7.0.11-200.fc44.x86_64
tradeoffs: Rust only; requires aarch64 with NEON+PMULL or x86_64 with AVX2/ADX/BMI2/PCLMULQDQ (excludes older CPUs like Raspberry Pi 4); very new/unaudited; RSA key generation is not side-channel-safe; built primarily as a rustls CryptoProvider rather than a standalone TLS stack
caveats: Independent third-party blog by the wtx author, not a well-known suite; code is public in wtx-bench.tar.xz but rustc and OpenSSL versions are not stated. It times whole processes (startup, PEM decode, loopback TCP), and the OpenSSL-minus-Graviola gap is a near-constant 3.1-4.7 ms across all 45 combinations, which is consistent with a fixed per-process cost rather than faster handshake crypto; the author says the cause is unknown ("a missing compile flag, an internal misconfiguration, the openssl-sys crate or OpenSSL itself"). Graviola is fastest in only 16 of 45 combinations; ring matches or beats it on several, and aws-lc-rs beats it with ECDSA-P384 certificates. Numbers exist only in SVG bar charts (means of 10 runs). Graviola's own jbp.io/graviola page (Ryzen 9 7940HS, Apple M2, no compiler/flags) compares only against ring, aws-lc-rs, rustcrypto, golang, dalek and libcrux, not OpenSSL. GitHub reports the license as NOASSERTION; LICENSE and Cargo.toml give 'Apache-2.0 OR ISC OR MIT-0' (the LICENSE prose says 'MIT license' but the included text is MIT-0).
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): HN Algolia query "TLS handshake performance" -> c410-f3r blog post; cross-checked via gh search repos "graviola" and gh api repos/ctz/graviola

verification.tier_reason: The c410-f3r blog compares aws-lc-rs, Graviola, ring and OpenSSL as swappable crypto backends of the wtx TLS stack; its code is public (wtx-bench.tar.xz: assets/bench.sh, src/main.rs, Cargo.toml profile 'deploy' opt-level=3/LTO/CGU1) and the CPU is stated (Ryzen 9 5900X), but no rustc or OpenSSL version is given, so it is not A. It is a personal blog by the wtx author (wtx 401 stars), not a well-known independent suite, so it is not B (same rule as quicperf and gonwan/webframework-benchmark).
verification.notes: Real independent comparison against OpenSSL, but it comes from a small personal harness without compiler versions, and the OpenSSL gap looks like fixed process overhead, so the tier drops from B to C. The license is corrected from 'Apache-2.0 OR MIT OR ISC' to 'Apache-2.0 OR ISC OR MIT-0'. Stars (305), last commit (2026-08-24) and active status check out.

name: aws-lc-rs
workload: Whole-process wall time of one wtx-bench binary run (hyperfine -N, 10 warmup + 10 measured runs, mean): decode 3 PEM files, start a TCP server thread and a client thread, complete one TLS handshake, exit without application data. 36 builds (4 crypto backends aws-lc-rs/Graviola/ring/OpenSSL x 3 key agreements secp256r1/secp384r1/X25519 x 3 cipher suites) each run with 5 certificate types (ECDSA P-256, ECDSA P-384, Ed25519, RSA-PSS-SHA256, RSA-PSS-SHA384), inside the WTX project's pluggable crypto layer.
claimed_speedup: Whole-process handshake run time (hyperfine mean, lower is better), read from the page's SVG bar charts (derived from page data, about +/-0.01 ms): aws-lc-rs 1.38-6.71 ms vs OpenSSL 4.41-10.20 ms. aws-lc-rs is faster than OpenSSL in all 45 combinations, by 1.30x-3.44x (median about 2.95x), e.g. Ed25519 + X25519 + AES-128-GCM 1.38 vs 4.74 ms (3.44x), RSA-PSS-SHA384 + X25519 + AES-256-GCM 6.66 vs 8.68 ms (1.30x). With RSA-PSS-SHA384 certificates aws-lc-rs (6.4-6.7 ms) trails ring (4.9-6.5 ms) and Graviola (5.2-5.9 ms), matching the page text; with secp384r1 key agreement it is fastest or near-fastest.
compiler_and_flags: wtx-bench Cargo.toml (in the page's wtx-bench.tar.xz): cargo build --profile deploy, which inherits release with opt-level=3, lto=true, codegen-units=1, panic='abort', debug-assertions and overflow-checks off. Exact rustc version not stated (Cargo.toml only sets rust-version = 1.96; wtx is built with its 'nightly' feature). OpenSSL version and build flags not stated; the author says OpenSSL's result may come from 'a missing compile flag'. bench.sh sets AWS_LC_SYS_USE_SYSTEM=0 (vendored AWS-LC build).
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5900X 12-Core, Linux Fedora 7.0.11-200.fc44.x86_64, 32GB DDR4
stars_or_usage: 655 stars (Rust-bindings crate); underlying aws-lc C library used in production AWS TLS stacks
tradeoffs: Wraps the C aws-lc library via FFI; RSA-PSS handshake path is comparatively slower than ring/Graviola per this benchmark; larger binary footprint than pure-Rust alternatives.
caveats: Single blog benchmark by the WTX author. Numbers exist only as SVG bar charts; values here were read from bar geometry (plotters output, about 0.01 ms per pixel). It times whole processes (process start, PEM decoding, loopback TCP, one handshake), not crypto alone. OpenSSL's near-constant 2-5 ms penalty in every combination suggests fixed init or integration overhead, and the author says the cause is unknown (compile flag, misconfiguration, openssl-sys, or OpenSSL itself). Only 10 runs per point; rustc and OpenSSL versions unstated. aws-lc-rs is Rust bindings over AWS-LC (github.com/aws/aws-lc, already catalogued), so the crypto speed shown is AWS-LC's.
found_via: Hacker News: query 'TLS handshake performance' -> https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48890397 ("TLS Handshakes: Measuring the Performance of 4 Cryptography Libraries")

It is not a peer-reviewed paper or well-known suite, so not B; it measures whole-process time rather than isolated handshake cost.

name: Cloudflare ChaCha20-Poly1305 (sslconfig OpenSSL patch)
workload: TLS AEAD 'seal' operation with 13 bytes of associated data (matching TLS record framing), plaintext sizes 64-16384 bytes, cycles/byte on a Haswell CPU with AVX2.
claimed_speedup: Page: 'significantly outperforms OpenSSL [1.1.0-pre] for short records, and is slightly faster for longer records. The average performance advantage is 7%' (average across the 64 B to 16 KB record sizes graphed; cycles/byte for 'seal' with 13 bytes AAD on Haswell; graphs only, not tabulated). The page also says it gets 'below 2 cycles/byte' for large records. AES-128-GCM and AES-256-GCM still beat ChaCha20-Poly1305 for records larger than 320 bytes.
hardware: Haswell CPU with AVX2 (exact model not stated)
tradeoffs: x86-64 assembly only (Sandy Bridge+/AVX2 paths); this exact code (by Vlad Krasnov / Cloudflare, with Andy Polyakov) was subsequently merged upstream into OpenSSL itself, so modern OpenSSL/BoringSSL already ship an equivalent fast ChaCha20-Poly1305 path -- the speed advantage over *current* OpenSSL is likely gone.
caveats: Numbers are read off graphs in a 2016-04-04 blog post, not tabulated. Compiler, flags and exact CPU model ('a Haswell CPU') are not stated, so tier is capped at C. The baseline was pre-release OpenSSL 1.1.0, and the page does not say whether that baseline was generic C or assembly. The repository is mainly Cloudflare's nginx cipher configuration. The speed code is patches/openssl__chacha20_poly1305_draft_and_rfc_ossl102{f,g,j}.patch (Vlad Krasnov; adds an AVX2 chacha20_poly1305_x86_64.pl) against OpenSSL 1.0.2. The openssl__1.1.0_chacha20_poly1305.patch only changes cipher-preference logic in ssl/s3_lib.c. The same stitched assembly (Copyright 2015 CloudFlare, author Vlad Krasnov) is in BoringSSL crypto/cipher_extra/asm/chacha20_poly1305_x86_64.pl. Inclusion in upstream OpenSSL was not verified. The patches modify OpenSSL-licensed files, so the repository's BSD-3-Clause license does not cover the whole patched tree. This is mainly a historical result, not a current 'faster than OpenSSL' claim.
found_via: Blog fetch: WebFetch on Cloudflare blog post 'It takes two to ChaCha (Poly)' (blog.cloudflare.com/it-takes-two-to-chacha-poly/), found via query 'Cloudflare ChaCha20-Poly1305 TLS performance'

verification.tier_reason: The Cloudflare blog post (2016-04-04) gives first-party cycles/byte graphs against OpenSSL 1.1.0-pre on an unnamed Haswell CPU. It states 'the average performance advantage is 7%' and 'below 2 cycles/byte', but it names no compiler or flags, no exact CPU model, and no benchmark code, so tier C.
verification.notes: The record's '7% for short TLS records' misattributes the figure. The page gives 7% as the average over all sizes and calls the short-record gain 'significant'. The caveat's '2015' date is wrong: the post is dated 2016-04-04. Last commit is 2024-09-16, so status is stale, not finished. gh api was rate-limited, so metadata comes from the github.com pages (BSD-3-Clause, 1313 stars, not archived).

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: Average 7% faster than OpenSSL 1.1.0-pre's ChaCha20-Poly1305 for short TLS records; below 2 cycles/byte for large records (exact numbers shown only as graphs, not tabulated)
corrected_fields.stars_or_usage: 1.3k stars
corrected_fields.caveats: Numbers are read off a graph in the blog post, not tabulated; compiler and exact CPU model are not stated (tier capped at C). Historical result from 2015 comparing to a pre-release OpenSSL 1.1.0 that did not yet have this code; since the same assembly was later contributed upstream, this is mainly of historical/pedagogical interest now, not a currently-valid 'faster than OpenSSL' claim.

name: FreeBSD in-kernel TLS (kTLS) with NIC TLS offload
workload: 2015 paper: Netflix OpenConnect Appliance serving real Netflix video traffic over TLS, nginx preferring AES-NI AES-GCM, with a sysctl toggling in-kernel TLS sendfile against plain userspace OpenSSL on the same firmware image, measured over a night of production traffic. 2019 slides: Netflix nginx video serving at 90 Gb/s, comparing CPU use of software kTLS against Chelsio T6 NIC kTLS offload.
claimed_speedup: Netflix AsiaBSDCon 2015 paper (early in-kernel TLS prototype, 'SSLsendfile'): the same OCA Rev D serving real Netflix traffic with AES-GCM did 'about 9Gps' with in-kernel bulk encryption versus 'about 8.5GPS' with userspace nginx+OpenSSL (~1.06x, derived from page data). The authors call this 'a slight performance improvement'. The later EuroBSDCon 2019 FreeBSD 13 kTLS slides give only 90 Gb/s at 68% CPU (software kTLS) versus 35% CPU (Chelsio T6 NIC kTLS offload), with no userspace-OpenSSL number.
hardware: 2015 comparison: Netflix OCA 'Rev D', Intel Xeon E5-2650L (exact version not stated), 64 GB RAM, FreeBSD 10.1, nginx 1.5. 2019 slides: Intel Xeon E5-2697A v4 @ 2.60GHz (16 core/32 HTT), 128GB DDR4-2400, 1x100GbE (T6 NIC), 4x NVMe.
stars_or_usage: GitHub mirror freebsd/freebsd-src has 9,335 stars; kernel kTLS support added in r351522 (FreeBSD 13); used in production at Netflix
tradeoffs: FreeBSD/Linux kernel-specific (not portable to arbitrary C++ apps); NIC-offload path needs specific hardware (Chelsio T6, Mellanox ConnectX-6 DX); adds kernel attack surface for TLS handling; only covers the bulk-record encryption phase, handshake still uses userspace OpenSSL/rustls/etc.
caveats: The only measured head-to-head against userspace OpenSSL (about 8.5 to about 9 Gbps, ~6%, read from the 2015 paper text) is for Netflix's early FreeBSD 10 prototype. That prototype still made an extra copy through the Open Crypto Framework, so it is not the FreeBSD 13 kTLS code now in freebsd-src (uipc_ktls.c, Copyright 2014-2019 Netflix). The 2019 slides compare software kTLS with NIC-offload kTLS only and argue the OpenSSL advantage qualitatively. The numbers are from live production traffic with no public benchmark harness or compiler details, so tier is capped at C. The kTLS files carry an SPDX BSD-2-Clause header. The repository-level license is NOASSERTION because FreeBSD mixes licenses.
found_via: Blog/talk fetch: HN Algolia query 'kernel TLS kTLS performance' -> Netflix/Mellanox/Chelsio conference slide deck 'Kernel TLS and hardware TLS offload in FreeBSD 13' at https://people.freebsd.org/~gallatin/talks/euro2019-ktls.pdf

verification.tier_reason: The EuroBSDCon 2019 slides only compare software kTLS (68% CPU) with T6 NIC kTLS (35% CPU) at 90 Gb/s. The Netflix AsiaBSDCon 2015 paper does compare against userspace nginx+OpenSSL on the same appliance with live traffic: about 8.5 Gbps versus about 9 Gbps with in-kernel TLS sendfile. These are first-party production numbers with no benchmark code or compiler details, so tier C.
verification.notes: The given benchmark_url has no numbers against the named OpenSSL baseline. I repointed benchmark_url to the Netflix AsiaBSDCon 2015 paper, which does measure against userspace nginx+OpenSSL, though only for a precursor prototype. The Netflix tech blog post on kTLS (Medium) returned 403 and was not read. gh api was rate-limited, so metadata comes from github.com pages (9335 stars, not archived, last commit on main 2026-09-26; uipc_ktls.c last changed 2026-09-23).

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: At the same 90Gb/s throughput: 68% CPU with software kTLS vs 35% CPU with Chelsio T6 NIC kTLS offload; software kTLS itself is motivated as retaining async sendfile(9)'s advantages (fewer context switches, no extra memory copy) that plain userspace OpenSSL + sendfile cannot get because OpenSSL's BIO datapath requires a userspace pointer to encrypt into.
corrected_fields.workload: Netflix nginx video-serving appliance streaming TLS-encrypted video at ~90 Gb/s over a single 100GbE NIC, comparing CPU utilization needed to sustain that rate with software kTLS record framing/encryption vs. Chelsio T6 NIC hardware TLS offload (both replacing plain userspace OpenSSL AES-NI + sendfile).
corrected_fields.hardware: Netflix ~2016 100G NVMe flash appliance: Intel Xeon E5-2697A v4 @ 2.60GHz (16 core/32 HTT), 128GB DDR4-2400, 1x100GbE NIC (Chelsio T6), 4x NVMe
corrected_fields.stars_or_usage: merged into FreeBSD 13 base system (r351522); used in production at Netflix
corrected_fields.caveats: The talk's only head-to-head numbers (68% vs 35% CPU at 90Gb/s) compare software kTLS to hardware-NIC kTLS, not directly to a measured plain-userspace-OpenSSL-with-sendfile baseline; the OpenSSL comparison is argued qualitatively (BIO datapath requires userspace copies) rather than benchmarked with a specific number on this slide deck. Capped at tier C for that reason.

name: OpenSSLNTRU (libsntrup761 + engntru OpenSSL ENGINE)
baseline: OpenSSL TLS 1.3 key exchange (ASM-optimized X25519 and P-256)
workload: Custom ~300-line tls_timer client performs 8,192 sequential TLS 1.3 handshakes between an Intel Core i7-6700 client and an AMD Ryzen 7 2700X server over Gigabit Ethernet, measuring average connections/sec; separately, cycle-counted key generation on a Haswell CPU.
claimed_speedup: USENIX Security '22 paper, Section 4.4 and Figure 5: over 100 samples of 8192 sequential TLS 1.3 handshakes each, sntrup761 and sntrup857 'consistently achieve more connections per second' than OpenSSL 1.1.1k's ASM-optimized X25519 and P-256. The results are shown only as CDF curves on a 440-620 connections/sec axis, with no tabulated numbers. Key generation: sntrup761 batch keygen (batch size 32) costs 156317 amortized Haswell cycles per key, versus 814608 for the previous best sntrup761 software and 269191 for CECPQ2's ntruhrss701 (~1.72x versus ntruhrss701, derived from page data). The ntruhrss701 comparison is against the CECPQ2 KEM, not against OpenSSL.
hardware: Client: Intel Core i7-6700; Server: AMD Ryzen 7 2700X; key-generation cycle counts measured on Haswell
tradeoffs: Requires patching OpenSSL (1.1.1f-1.1.1m only, not tested against 3.x); post-quantum-only KEM, not a general TLS library; experimental/demo-quality integration; no formal security audit of engntru/libsntrup761.
caveats: The paper was published at USENIX Security 2022 (confirmed on the usenix.org presentation page, with Available, Functional and Reproduced artifact badges). The headline 'more handshakes/sec' result is shown only as a CDF plot, not a tabulated number. The authors warn that 'one should not conclude that sntrup761 and sntrup857 cost less than ECC overall', because the unloaded Gigabit LAN hides the larger lattice communication costs. The 156317-cycle figure is the amortized cost of batch key generation (batch of 32); unbatched sntrup761 keygen is 819332 cycles (Table 3). Licensing is mixed: engntru is LGPL-3.0-or-later (COPYING and COPYING.LESSER), tls_timer is Apache-2.0 (LICENSE), and the speed-critical libsntrup761 tarball has no license file or statement (only build and test harness files say 'Public domain'). The OpenSSL patches modify OpenSSL 1.1.1 code. The demo page was last updated 2021.12.14 (OpenSSL 1.1.1m patch); the library tarballs are dated 2021-06-08.
found_via: arXiv API search 'all:TLS AND all:OpenSSL AND all:performance' -> arXiv:2106.08759 'OpenSSLNTRU: Faster post-quantum TLS key exchange' -> https://opensslntru.cr.yp.to

verification.tier_reason: The paper appeared at USENIX Security '22 (peer-reviewed; artifact badges Available, Functional and Reproduced). Its Section 4.4 and Figure 5 show sntrup761 and sntrup857 completing more TLS 1.3 connections/sec than OpenSSL 1.1.1k's ASM-optimized X25519 and P-256, with tls_timer code public and CPUs named. Compiler and flags are not stated, so not A. This upgrades the record from C to B.
verification.notes: The given demo.html only carries the 156317-cycle keygen figure. The X25519/P-256 handshake comparison is in the paper, and the 269191 ntruhrss701 figure is on the intro page and in paper Table 1, so I repointed benchmark_url to the paper PDF. The venue is confirmed as USENIX Security '22, which moves the tier from C to B. The record's claim that no license exists in the tarballs is wrong for engntru (LGPL-3.0+) and tls_timer (Apache-2.0). I kept usability 'reference' because the core libsntrup761 is unlicensed, and set status to abandoned because the last update was more than 3 years ago and the authors do not say the work is complete.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: sntrup761 post-quantum KEM completes more TLS 1.3 sessions/sec than OpenSSL 1.1.1k's ASM-optimized X25519 and P-256 (reported as CDF curves, not tabulated numbers); key generation takes 156317 Haswell cycles vs 269191 for the earlier CECPQ2 ntruhrss701 KEM (~1.7x faster keygen)

Bernstein et al. and may have appeared in a peer-reviewed venue, but venue could not be independently confirmed this session (Semantic Scholar/DBLP fetches were blocked/rate-limited), so it is scored as a first-party claim (tier C) rather than tier B. name: picotls "fusion" AES-GCM engine
workload: AES-GCM AEAD encryption throughput (bytes/s) for QUIC-sized 1440-byte blocks and 16KB blocks, with 13-byte AAD. fusionbench.c uses a 16-byte key, so this is AES-128-GCM; the chart does not label the key size, and AES-256 support was still a to-do in the PR. The chart also shows fusion with QUIC header protection computed in parallel.
claimed_speedup: At 1440-byte AEAD blocks, fusion's throughput is 5.86e9 vs 4.43e9 B/s on Core i5 9400 (1.32x), 4.91e9 vs 3.61e9 on Ryzen 3 3200G (1.36x) and 3.07e9 vs 2.32e9 on Core m3 6Y30 (1.32x). The baseline is OpenSSL 1.1.1g in full-AEAD mode (derived from page data). At 16384-byte blocks the gap shrinks to 1.01-1.15x. The PR text itself says OpenSSL loses ~30% throughput at 1440 bytes compared with 16KB, while fusion cuts that overhead to ~10%. Against OpenSSL's AES-GCM-core-only numbers (no AAD, IV setup or finalization), fusion at 1440 bytes is 1.03-1.14x.
hardware: Intel Core i5 9400 @4GHz, AMD Ryzen 3 3200G @3.6GHz, Intel Core m3 6Y30 @2.2GHz (chart labels in the PR)
stars_or_usage: 641 stars; used in the H2O HTTP server
tradeoffs: Fusion is x86-64-specific and written in plain C (not hand assembly) to keep pipelines full for short AEAD blocks; it's one of four interchangeable crypto backends in picotls (OpenSSL, minicrypto, fusion, libaegis), so using it is opt-in and the OpenSSL backend remains the default for portability.
caveats: The PR states no compiler or flags, and the chart gives no cycles/byte. The CPU models are on the chart, contrary to the original record. The baseline is OpenSSL 1.1.1g from 2020, now several major releases old, and OpenSSL was measured with `openssl speed -aead` rather than the same harness as fusion. The win is mainly at short (QUIC-sized) blocks, 1.3x or more; at 16KB it is 1-15%. Fusion is x86-64 only and needs AES-NI, PCLMUL and AVX2. The repo has no top-level LICENSE file. The README says MIT, and lib/fusion.c is under both Apache-2.0 and MIT because its transformH function is derived from OpenSSL. The minicrypto binding pulls in cifra (CC0; no patent grant) and micro-ecc (BSD-2-Clause). The repo's t/ptlsbench.c now benchmarks fusion and OpenSSL AEADs side by side, but no published results with methodology were found.

Metadata checked with gh: 641 stars, not a fork, not archived, last commit 2026-09-25.

name: ring
workload: Whole-process wall time of one wtx-bench binary run (hyperfine -N, 10 warmup + 10 measured runs, mean): decode 3 PEM files, start a TCP server thread and a client thread, complete one TLS handshake, exit without application data. 36 builds (4 crypto backends aws-lc-rs/Graviola/ring/OpenSSL x 3 key agreements secp256r1/secp384r1/X25519 x 3 cipher suites) each run with 5 certificate types (ECDSA P-256, ECDSA P-384, Ed25519, RSA-PSS-SHA256, RSA-PSS-SHA384), inside the WTX project's pluggable crypto layer.
claimed_speedup: Whole-process handshake run time (hyperfine mean, lower is better), read from the page's SVG bar charts (derived from page data, about +/-0.01 ms): ring 1.29-6.50 ms vs OpenSSL 4.41-10.20 ms. ring is faster than OpenSSL in all 45 combinations, by 1.47x-3.67x (median about 2.15x), e.g. Ed25519 + X25519 + AES-128-GCM 1.29 vs 4.74 ms (3.67x), ECDSA-P384 + secp384r1 + AES-128-GCM 4.77 vs 7.03 ms (1.47x). ring is the fastest of the 4 libraries in 16 of 45 combinations (none with secp384r1, where it trails aws-lc-rs by up to about 2.2x). Page text: 'OpenSSL is the slower library'; room for optimization in secp384r1 'for both OpenSSL and ring'.
compiler_and_flags: wtx-bench Cargo.toml (in the page's wtx-bench.tar.xz): cargo build --profile deploy, which inherits release with opt-level=3, lto=true, codegen-units=1, panic='abort', debug-assertions and overflow-checks off. Exact rustc version not stated (Cargo.toml only sets rust-version = 1.96; wtx is built with its 'nightly' feature). OpenSSL version and build flags not stated; the author says OpenSSL's result may come from 'a missing compile flag'.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5900X 12-Core, Linux Fedora 7.0.11-200.fc44.x86_64, 32GB DDR4
license: Apache-2.0 AND ISC (ring's own code ISC; BoringSSL-derived code Apache-2.0 per LICENSE-BoringSSL; once_cell polyfill Apache-2.0/MIT)
stars_or_usage: 4.1k stars; used transitively via rustls/quinn/tokio ecosystem
tradeoffs: Deliberately minimal, low-level unsafe-adjacent API by design (no general-purpose TLS API of its own); non-standard composite license complicates SPDX classification/compliance tooling.
caveats: Single blog benchmark by the WTX author. Numbers exist only as SVG bar charts; values here were read from bar geometry (plotters output, about 0.01 ms per pixel). It times whole processes (process start, PEM decoding, loopback TCP, one handshake), not crypto alone. OpenSSL's near-constant 2-4.4 ms penalty against ring in every combination suggests fixed init or integration overhead, and the author says the cause is unknown (compile flag, misconfiguration, openssl-sys, or OpenSSL itself). Only 10 runs per point; rustc and OpenSSL versions unstated. ring is slow with secp384r1 key agreement.
found_via: Hacker News: query 'TLS handshake performance' -> https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48890397 ("TLS Handshakes: Measuring the Performance of 4 Cryptography Libraries")

name: Tempesta FW (Tempesta TLS)
workload: Server-side full and abbreviated TLS 1.2 handshakes (ECDHE+ECDSA over NIST P-256) measured with the project's own tls-perf tool and wrk, comparing Nginx 1.19.1/OpenSSL 1.1.1d against Tempesta FW's in-Linux-kernel TLS handshake implementation, on a 1-vCPU KVM VM and on 2-node bare-metal servers
claimed_speedup: 40-80% more TLS connections/sec than Nginx/OpenSSL and up to 4x lower latency in some tests; concretely: 1-CPU VM new-session RPS 2,180 vs 1,545 (+41%), avg latency 307ms vs 1,340ms (-77%); 2-CPU bare-metal session-resumption 35,263 vs 19,203 conn/s (+83%); 2-CPU bare-metal new-session RPS only 7,921 vs 7,426 (+6%). Raw crypto op/s were slower than OpenSSL: ECDSA 27,261 vs OpenSSL's 36,472 op/s, ECDHE 6,690 vs OpenSSL's 16,619 op/s -- the throughput win comes from avoiding user/kernel context switches and heap allocation, not from faster math.
hardware: 1 vCPU KVM VM on Intel Core i7-6500U host (no vAPIC), virtio_net; 2-node bare-metal cluster with Intel Xeon E3-1240v5 CPUs and Mellanox ConnectX-2 10GbE, Linux kernel 5.7 (also compared to 4.14)
tradeoffs: Linux-kernel-only (x86-64 with AVX/BMI/ADX required, no generic C fallback for the crypto routines), puts TLS handshake code in kernel space (larger attack surface / TCB), GPLv2 licensing, and the paper itself reports tail-latency spikes up to 30x worse in the worst case on bare metal under SoftIRQ load
caveats: This is a first-party paper/benchmark by the Tempesta Technologies team (NetDev 0x14 conference paper, July 2020), not independent peer review, so it is capped at tier C despite the public benchmark tool (tls-perf) and stated hardware; compiler and build flags are not given. The headline 40-80% figure applies mainly to the 1-vCPU VM and to session resumption; the bare-metal new-session gain was only +6%. On bare metal Nginx/OpenSSL had lower average and 95th-percentile latency (the paper says 50-170% lower for new sessions and 4-9% for resumption), and Tempesta showed large tail-latency spikes (max latency up to +3000%, 28,262 vs 925 ms on resumption). The raw ECDSA/ECDHE op/s were lower than OpenSSL even though Tempesta's figures include ephemeral key generation, so that comparison is not like-for-like. Only x86-64 with AVX/BMI/ADX is supported, and the design relies on RDRAND randomization, which SRBDS microcode mitigations slow. Test hardware and kernel (5.7, 2020) are dated, and the code has changed since.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "tempesta" --sort stars; paper found via HN Algolia query "TLS faster than OpenSSL" -> https://netdevconf.info/0x14/pub/papers/35/0x14-paper35-talk-paper.pdf
GitHub: tempesta-tech/tempesta README 'x3 faster than Nginx' claim -> linked knowledge-base Performance / HTTP-transactions-performance pages

name: cmd-stream (with MUS codec)
workload: Echo-style Distributed-Command-Pattern RPC over TCP with 30ms simulated server processing delay, payloads 17-1024 bytes, 1/2/4/8/16 concurrent client goroutines (go test -bench BenchmarkQPS).
claimed_speedup: ~3.15x more QPS than grpc-go/Protobuf at 1 client (145,352 vs 46,142 QPS) rising to ~4.56x at 16 clients (288,727 vs 63,285 QPS) (derived from page data: results/qps/qps.csv)
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.24.1; go test -bench BenchmarkQPS -count=10 -timeout=30m
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 PRO 5850U with Radeon Graphics, Debian 6.1.148-1 x86_64 (single laptop, charger connected, fan at full speed)
tradeoffs: Custom Distributed Command Pattern rather than classic request/response RPC; peak speedup requires the companion MUS binary codec (codec-mus-stream-go), which needs code generation; JSON codec variant is much closer to gRPC in throughput.
caveats: The benchmark repo (ymz-ncnk/go-client-server-benchmarks, 17 stars) is maintained by the cmd-stream author, so it is not independent. Methodology, code, Go version and CPU are fully disclosed, so it stays at tier A. The run is on a single laptop, not a controlled server, and no variance is reported beyond -count=10. The comparison is cmd-stream over raw TCP against gRPC over HTTP/2. The protobuf codec on cmd-stream also beats gRPC (108788 vs 46142 QPS at 1 client), so most of the gain comes from the transport, not from the MUS codec. The fixed-count run (100,000 requests, sec.csv) shows a smaller gap: 0.612s vs 2.091s at 1 client (~3.4x) and 0.383s vs 1.033s at 16 clients (~2.7x).

name: Homa (HomaModule) — Linux kernel implementation of the Homa RPC transport protocol
workload: 40-node CloudLab cluster; basic back-to-back single-client RPC latency/throughput (Table 2) plus four of the 'Montazeri' request/response workloads under high network load, measuring P50/P99/P999 tail latency across message sizes; Homa is explicitly designed as a transport for datacenter RPC frameworks (paper names gRPC and Apache Thrift as the frameworks it targets)
claimed_speedup: 40-node cluster benchmark at high load (workloads W2-W5): for short messages, P99 latency is 19-72x lower than TCP and 7-83x lower than DCTCP (the abstract summarises this as 7-83x lower than TCP and DCTCP). For short messages, P50 is 3.5-7.5x lower than TCP and 2.7-3.8x lower than DCTCP. Homa's P50 and P99 are lower than TCP/DCTCP at every message size, but the 7-83x range applies only to short messages. Best-case 100-byte RTT: 15.1us (Homa) vs 23.4us (TCP) vs 24.1us (DCTCP). Client and server RPC rate: 1.6 vs 1.0 Mops/sec (60% higher).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the paper. The kernel module is built with kbuild against Linux 5.4.80 using the kernel's own flags. The repo's current util/Makefile builds the cp_node benchmark driver with g++ -Wall -Werror -fno-strict-aliasing -O3. No compiler version is given anywhere.
hardware: CloudLab xl170 nodes: Intel Xeon E5-2640v4 (10 cores, 2.4GHz), 4x16GB DDR4-2400, Intel DC S3520 480GB SSD, Mellanox ConnectX-4 25Gbps NIC, Mellanox 2410 switch, 40-node cluster
license: BSD-2-Clause OR GPL-2.0+ (per-file SPDX headers on the module and benchmark sources; a few test/tool files are BSD-1-Clause or GPL-2.0; no top-level LICENSE file)
tradeoffs: Requires a custom Linux kernel module (no macOS/Windows, no unprivileged/userspace-only path); new homa_send/homa_recv/homa_reply socket API is not backward-compatible with existing TCP/UDP socket code, so gRPC/Thrift apps need a shim (see grpc_homa) to use it transparently; needs specific NIC support (Mellanox ConnectX-4/5/6, Intel E810 verified); paper states small-message throughput is still 5-10x below raw NIC line rate due to software/kernel overhead.
caveats: The 7-83x win is for P99 latency of short messages under high load, not for raw bandwidth. The paper's own Table 2 shows single-connection 500KB throughput where Homa (10.0 Gbps) is LOWER than TCP (20.3 Gbps); multi-RPC throughput is equal (23.8 vs 23.9 Gbps). The baseline is Linux kernel TCP/DCTCP, not gRPC or Thrift themselves; the RPC-framework link goes through the separate, less mature PlatformLab/grpc_homa shim (reported as a companion entry). The paper's numbers come from the 2021 code on Linux 5.4.80. The module has since been heavily reworked (Homa 2.0, sendmsg/recvmsg API, Linux 6.17.8, upstreaming under way since Oct 2024), so current performance may differ. The license exists only in per-file SPDX headers (no LICENSE file).
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "Homa transport" -> PlatformLab/HomaModule; paper linked from repo README (USENIX ATC 2021, https://www.usenix.org/system/files/atc21-ousterhout.pdf)

verification.tier_reason: Peer-reviewed USENIX ATC 2021 paper compares Homa/Linux directly against Linux kernel TCP and DCTCP. The hardware is fully stated (Table 1: CloudLab xl170, Xeon E5-2640v4, ConnectX-4 25 Gbps, Linux 5.4.80), and the benchmark code is public (util/cp_node.cc driven by util/cp_bench, which the README says produced Figs 3-4). The compiler and flags are never stated for the kernel module or the kernel, so this falls short of A.
verification.notes: The paper's text is 'P99 19-72x lower than TCP and 7-83x lower than DCTCP' for short messages. The record's 'across all message sizes' overstated the 7-83x range, so claimed_speedup was corrected. The GitHub API reports license null, but a scan of 106 code files found SPDX 'BSD-2-Clause OR GPL-2.0+' on 93 of them. The rest are BSD-1-Clause, GPL, xxhash BSD-2 or a dual-licensed Wireshark dissector, plus one scratch.c/avg.py with no header, so usability is copyable. Metadata checked: 435 stars, not archived, not a fork, last commit 2026-09-25.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: P99 tail latency 7-83x lower than TCP and DCTCP across all message sizes under high load; basic 100-byte RPC latency 15.1us (Homa) vs 23.4us (TCP) vs 24.1us (DCTCP); client RPC rate 1.6 Mops/sec (Homa) vs 1.0 Mops/sec (TCP)
corrected_fields.compiler_and_flags: Linux kernel module built against Linux 5.4.80 via the repo's standard kernel Makefile; no userspace optimization flags reported (kernel-module benchmark, not a userspace std-facility comparison)

Baseline compared directly is TCP/DCTCP, not gRPC or Thrift themselves; the RPC-framework connection is via the separate, less mature PlatformLab/grpc_homa shim (reported as a companion entry).

name: rpcx
baseline: gRPC (grpc-go 1.39.0); also Go standard library net/rpc (Go 1.16.6)
workload: Synchronous RPC with a 581-byte Protobuf BenchmarkMessage: the server sets one field to OK and returns it. Client and server run on the same machine over loopback, with a shared client pool and warmup. Each scenario sends 10,000,000 requests at 100/200/500/1000/2000/5000 concurrent clients, with no simulated processing delay.
claimed_speedup: ~2.3x-2.6x higher throughput than grpc-go 1.39.0 across 100-5000 concurrent clients (249,308 vs 96,463 TPS at 100; 303,287 vs 116,608 at 1000; 317,874 vs 136,108 at 2000; 315,397 vs 121,989 at 5000), and ~1.3x-1.5x over the Go standard library net/rpc (249,308 vs 189,221 at 100; 315,397 vs 204,503 at 5000) (derived from page data: the raw-data table image data.png on the 2021 post)
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.16.6; rpcx 1.6.5, grpc 1.39.0, go std rpc 1.16.6, kitex 0.0.3, arpc 1.1.5; run as ./xxx_server -d 127.0.0.1:8972 and ./xxx_client -c <concurrency> -n 10000000 -s 127.0.0.1:8973 (go build flags not stated)
hardware: Intel Xeon Silver 4110 @ 2.10GHz, 2 sockets (the post states 8 physical cores and 32 logical cores with hyper-threading), 128GB RAM; client and server on the same machine over loopback
tradeoffs: Uses its own service-discovery/governance stack (zookeeper/etcd/consul) layered on top of the RPC core; multiple codecs supported (Protobuf/JSON/MessagePack) with the compared numbers specific to Protobuf.
caveats: All results are first-party: the rpcx author runs the benchmark and publishes it on his blog, colobu.com. The rounds in the same benchmark project disagree. The 2018 chart (Go 1.9.0, E5-2630 v3; linked from the rpcx README) shows ~1.5x over grpc-go (~205k/199k/200k vs ~135k/131k/129k calls/s at 500/2000/5000 clients) and ~2.7-2.9x over Thrift (~75k/70k/72k). In that round the Go standard library net/rpc (~290k) beat rpcx. The 2019 table in the rpcx-ecosystem/rpcx-benchmark README has grpc ahead at 256 concurrency (130,642 vs 122,166 TPS) and rpcx only ~1.15x ahead at 512/1024. The 2020 test_data.md has grpc ahead at c=100 (108,928 vs 100,926) and rpcx 1.30x ahead at c=1000 (171,600 vs 132,037). The size of the gap therefore depends heavily on the round, the hardware and the concurrency. The 2021 numbers are in an image table only. HEAD of rpcxio/rpcx-benchmark has since moved to grpc v1.48.0 and rpcx v1.8.33, so reproducing the exact run needs commit 699aab8d. GitHub's license API reports NOASSERTION, but the LICENSE file is the standard Apache License 2.0 notice (Copyright 2017 Chao yuepan).
