name: sockudo-ws
workload: Plaintext WebSocket echo server driven by the uSockets load_test client from the denoland/fastwebsockets benches harness. Payloads are 512 and 1024 bytes at 100 and 500 concurrent connections, measured in messages/sec. These cases are not in the published run.js, which uses 20B/100, 1KB/10 and 16KB at 10/200/500, so a locally modified harness was used.
claimed_speedup: 1.02x-1.03x higher msg/s than uWebSockets v20.64 across the 4 tested cases (e.g. 232,712 vs 227,973 msg/s at 512B/100 conns; 232,072 vs 224,498 msg/s at 1024B/100 conns; 231,135 vs 222,493 msg/s at 512B/500 conns; 222,578 vs 216,833 msg/s at 1024B/500 conns)
compiler_and_flags: README states Rust 1.82 and uWebSockets v20.64, but the crate has used edition = "2024" (needs Rust >= 1.85) since its initial commit, so the stated toolchain is inconsistent. Build flags for sockudo-ws and the C++ compiler/flags for the uWebSockets EchoServer are not stated for this comparison. The harness load_test.c client is built with clang -flto -O3 per the fastwebsockets benches Makefile.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, 32GB RAM, Linux 6.18
tradeoffs: Rust safety/ergonomics vs uWebSockets' raw C++ API; sockudo-ws is a newer, much less battle-tested library than uWebSockets, which underpins many production Node.js/Bun stacks.
caveats: The margin over uWebSockets is only 2-3%, which is within plausible run-to-run noise for a single-machine run. No repeated runs or variance are reported. The numbers are self-reported and have not changed since the repo's initial commit (2025-12-29), while the library has since gone from v1.x to v2.1.0. The harness is third-party (denoland/fastwebsockets benches), but the sockudo-ws target, its echo server and the modified cases are not published, so the run cannot be reproduced as stated. The environment line (Ryzen 9 7950X, Linux 6.18, Rust 1.82) was added after the numbers. Rust 1.82 cannot compile this edition-2024 crate. No build flags for either side are given.

compiler_and_flags: wtx: Rust nightly-2026-06-27 (rust:1.95 base image), `RUSTFLAGS="-C target-cpu=native" cargo build --release` with release profile opt-level=3, lto="thin", codegen-units=1, panic="abort"; wtx 0.49 (features grpc-server, optimizations-std, quick-protobuf, tokio) per frameworks/wtx-grpc/Dockerfile and Cargo.toml in MDA2AV/HttpArena. grpc-go: Go 1.24 (golang:1.24-bookworm image), `CGO_ENABLED=0 go build`, google.golang.org/grpc v1.72.0, default grpc.NewServer() with GOMAXPROCS=NumCPU (frameworks/grpc-go).
hardware: AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 3995WX (Zen 2, 64 cores / 128 threads, single NUMA node, performance governor). Per HttpArena's Hardware & Topology docs, the server is pinned to a 64-thread cpuset (0-31,64-95 = 32 physical cores plus SMT siblings) and the load generator to the other half of the same chip; every run uses the same machine.
tradeoffs: wtx is a multi-protocol crate (gRPC, HTTP/2, WebSocket, Postgres, TLS, etc.) rather than a dedicated RPC-only library; requires nightly Rust; small community and, per its own README, 'not widely used and has not undergone security audits'; used noticeably more memory (727MiB-1022MiB) than grpc-go (310-922MiB) in this test.
caveats: wtx's server process used ~64 logical CPUs (6379-6383% cpu) versus grpc-go's ~44 (4339-4478% cpu) during the run, so throughput-per-core is not directly comparable, only end-to-end rps on shared hardware. The two results were not measured in the same session: grpc-go's unary-grpc numbers have been unchanged since an HttpArena results update on 2026-04-12 (commit f326f067), while wtx's current numbers come from a re-run on 2026-08-24 (PR #1300), and the harness evolved in between. wtx's earlier published unary-grpc numbers (2026-07-30 to 2026-08-24) were invalid: its handler returned an empty reply body that h2load did not detect; body validation caught it, the entry was disabled (PR #1291), fixed and re-validated in PR #1300. The figures above are the post-fix validated numbers. The harness (HttpArena, github.com/MDA2AV/HttpArena, MIT-licensed) is a general full-stack web-framework benchmark, not an RPC-specific shootout. The wtx-grpc entry was contributed by wtx's own author (c410-f3r, PRs #812 and #1056), so it is not a fully arms-length third party, although the Dockerfiles, build commands and raw JSON results are public and runs are done centrally by the HttpArena maintainers. grpc-go is labeled 'tuned' but runs a default grpc.NewServer(). tonic (Rust's main gRPC framework) has a directory in the repo and was benchmarked in an April 2026 pre-round (378,723 rps at 256 connections, commit 2b36f907), but it is absent from the current results, so no current same-language comparison exists. wtx is not the fastest entry on the board: zix, cardigan and swerver post about 6.8-7.0M rps in the same test.

name: Lightstream
workload: Streaming RAM-resident Apache Arrow tables (numeric, mixed, string-heavy, wide schemas; 1M rows/batch from a 300GB pool) between two AWS instances over a 50 Gbit/s network, across multiple levels of connection parallelism
claimed_speedup: Warm-median throughput (median of 5 runs, GiB/s) is 1.06x-1.71x Arrow Flight in all 16 cells (4 schema shapes x 1/4/8/16 streams). For example, numeric with 1 stream: 1.109 vs 0.649 GiB/s (1.71x); numeric with 16 streams: 5.780 vs 5.434 (1.06x); string-heavy with 1 stream: 1.109 vs 0.828 (1.34x). The gap narrows toward the 50 Gbit/s link limit as stream count rises. No numeric latency comparison is given in text, only the claim that p99 is within 1% of p50.
compiler_and_flags: Rust nightly (rustlang/rust:nightly-bookworm-slim Docker image, version not pinned), cargo build --release, features bench_arrow_flight,protocol,tcp,mmap (rust/benches/ecs/Dockerfile)
hardware: 2x AWS i3en.12xlarge instances in one placement group, 50 Gbit/s network
tradeoffs: Purpose-built for bulk columnar Arrow-table transport, not a general RPC replacement; Lightstream reconstructs one globally-ordered stream across parallel connections, a cost the README says it 'wears' in its own reported numbers, while Arrow Flight orders only per-endpoint
caveats: Baseline is Arrow Flight (the arrow-flight crate over gRPC/HTTP2), not bare gRPC, so this is a proxy comparison. First-party benchmark; the code is in rust/benches/ecs/. The README says 'see benchmarks/', but that root path does not exist. The CPU model is not stated (only the i3en.12xlarge instance type) and the nightly toolchain is not pinned. Gains shrink to 1.06x-1.17x at 16 streams, where both approach the 50 Gbit/s link. Lightstream's timing includes global ordered reconstruction, which Flight does not do. The project is very new and has no independent reproduction.

name: ActualLab.Rpc (part of ActualLab.Fusion)
workload: Client/server RPC over Windows localhost loopback (not in-process): unary calls Sum/GetUser/SayHello (calls/s) and server streaming of 1-byte/100-byte/10KB items (items/s); plus a Docker run with a 4-CPU server matching grpc_bench's SayHello setup. ActualLab.Rpc uses its msgpack6c serializer; gRPC is grpc-dotnet (Grpc.AspNetCore).
claimed_speedup: Localhost calls: Sum 9.91M calls/s vs gRPC 1.28M (~7.7x) and SignalR 4.85M; GetUser 8.75M vs gRPC 1.24M (~7.1x); SayHello 6.04M vs gRPC 1.16M (~5.2x). Streams: Stream1 99.96M items/s vs gRPC 43.78M (~2.3x); Stream100 44.89M vs 25.87M (~1.7x); Stream10K 807.84K vs 572.76K (~1.4x). Docker 4-CPU server: SayHello 2.52M vs gRPC 399.32K calls/s (~6.3x, stated on page). Speedup ranges are printed on docs/Performance.md. README says "2-7x faster than gRPC and SignalR even in its 'raw' mode".
compiler_and_flags: .NET 10.0.8 (Docker runs: .NET 10 SDK image 10.0.10); dotnet run -c Release; RpcBenchmark.csproj sets TieredPGO=true, TieredCompilation + QuickJit/QuickJitForLoops=true, ServerGarbageCollection=true, RetainVMGarbageCollection=true, GarbageCollectionAdaptationMode=0; args: test -b calls|streams -l rpc,grpc,signalr -f msgpack6c -s -n 6
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D (16C/32T), 96 GB DDR5, Windows 11; localhost loopback with Windows loopback large MTU enabled. Docker variant: server container limited to 4 CPUs, clients 24 CPUs.
tradeoffs: .NET/C# only; part of a larger real-time framework (Fusion) with its own caching/pub-sub model, so adopting ActualLab.Rpc in isolation is less common; API differs substantially from gRPC's contract-first model
caveats: First-party benchmark (harness lives in the separate ActualLab/Fusion.Samples repo, MIT, 17 stars). name: brpc
workload: Same-machine and cross-machine RPC echo workloads: QPS vs request size, QPS vs thread count, and tail-latency CDFs under 1% long-tail requests, single-server and multi-hop server topologies
claimed_speedup: Page text: pooled brpc (baidu-rpc_mc) reached the highest throughput in the test, 2.3GB/s; gRPC 'was at the bottom in almost every test it took part in' and its cross-machine multi-client latency CDF 'is completely out of control' (the same-machine CDF test is where some gRPC requests timed out). Read off the charts (derived from page data): same-machine 16B requests, brpc single-connection ~216k QPS vs gRPC ~33k (~6.5x) and thrift_mc ~71k (~3x); 1KB requests at 256 client threads, brpc ~291k vs gRPC ~32k (~9x) and thrift_mc ~70k (~4x); cross-machine 32 clients, brpc ~950k vs gRPC ~39k (~24x) and thrift_mc ~93k (~10x). Versus Thrift the win is not uniform: thrift_mc and UB beat brpc at 1-8 client threads, and single-connection brpc falls below thrift_mc at 16KB+ requests (pooled brpc stays above). The page says Thrift's cross-machine average latency is clearly higher than brpc's.
hardware: Single machine: E5-2620 @ 2.00GHz, 24 cores with hyper-threading, 64GB RAM, Linux 2.6.32. Cluster 1: 15x E5-2420 @ 1.90GHz + 8x E5-2620 2.0GHz, 12 cores no HT, 1GbE. Cluster 2: 30x E5-2620 v3 @ 2.40GHz, 12 cores no HT, 96GB RAM, 10GbE.
tradeoffs: Historically closely tied to Baidu's internal protocols and tooling; heavier/more complex than lightweight RPC libs; primarily documented in Chinese.
caveats: Tests were run in 2015/early 2016 (charts timestamped 2016-01-22..24) and the page itself says they may not reflect the latest status. gRPC tested was release-0_11 (pre-1.0) and Thrift was an internal build of 0.9.1, so neither represents modern versions. gRPC was left out of the two multi-server latency tests. Compiler and build flags are not stated and the gRPC/Thrift server code used is not published. Thrift beats brpc at low client-thread counts (1-8) and against single-connection brpc at 16KB+ requests.

name: Machnet
baseline: Linux kernel TCP/IP stack (sockperf with Nagle disabled for microbenchmarks; kernel-TCP builds of a FASTER KV server and of Hashicorp Raft's transport)
workload: Round-trip latency of 64 B echo messages between two Azure F8s_v2 VMs in the same availability zone, one message in flight (Fig. 10). Also a single-threaded FASTER KV server doing 100% GETs over 100M 8-byte keys (Fig. 6), and Hashicorp's Go Raft replicating 80 B commands across 3 VMs (Fig. 8).
claimed_speedup: 'Linux TCP's latency is 2.6x, 4.2x, and 7.4x higher than Machnet at median, p99, and p99.9' (64 B echo; Machnet median 27 us). FASTER KV: '3.3x higher throughput, with 700K RPS compared to Linux TCP's 210K RPS', and at 210K RPS a p99 of 50 us vs 250 us (80% lower), using 2 cores vs 100% of all 8 for Linux. Go Raft: 34% lower median latency and 37% lower p99 (p50 185 us vs 282 us, p99 625 us vs 1000 us).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the paper. The repo's src/CMakeLists.txt Release build uses C++20 with -O3 -DNDEBUG -fno-rtti -fno-exceptions and needs DPDK 23.11. The Docker image builds on Ubuntu 22.04 with build-essential; no compiler version is pinned.
hardware: Azure F8s_v2 VMs (8 vCPUs, 16 GB DRAM) with accelerated networking, Ubuntu 22.04.2, Linux kernel 6.2, same region and availability zone, no proximity placement groups. Hugepages and pinned stack processes for the DPDK stacks; no isolcpus or IRQ steering. The CPU model is not stated. The repo's PERFORMANCE_REPORT lists the Azure F8s_v2 vNIC as CX4-Lx with the netvsc PMD.
stars_or_usage: 162 stars, 33 forks. eRPC's README opens with a Dec 2023 news line telling users to check out Machnet.
tradeoffs: Machnet runs as a separate busy-polling sidecar that takes at least one dedicated engine core. It needs a second, dedicated vNIC per VM that is unbound from the kernel, plus DPDK and hugepages; the prebuilt image comes from GHCR and needs a GitHub token. Apps use its own sockets-like shared-memory message API (machnet_attach/listen/connect/send/recv), not BSD sockets, so they must be ported (C shim with Go, Rust and JS bindings). Its reliable, connection-oriented message protocol only talks to other Machnet peers, so it cannot replace TCP for outside clients. In exchange it runs on basic cloud vNICs (Azure, AWS, GCP) without flow steering, and it supports multiple processes per NIC and blocking receives. Each shared-memory crossing costs ~250 ns, and new connections are handled on a 50 us periodic interval.
caveats: The numbers come from arXiv v1 (Feb 2025, 'Fast Userspace Networking for the Rest of Us', where the figures still label the system 'CNet'). The arXiv API shows no later version as of 2026-09-26. That is a pre-review, first-party version. The peer-reviewed paper is 'Enabling Fast Networking in the Public Cloud', ASPLOS '26, pp. 679-696, DOI 10.1145/3779212.3790158, with a changed author list. Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex mark it Gold OA (CC-BY), and the Machnet docs site links it, but dl.acm.org returned 403 and the PoliMi IRIS record has no file, so the final numbers are unverified. That is why this is tier C; it would be B if the ASPLOS text keeps these comparisons. The Linux baseline is kernel TCP via sockperf, which is not a listed websocket-grpc-rpc baseline (gRPC/uWebSockets/Thrift). That baseline is untuned: Nagle is off, but busy-polling sockets, isolcpus and IRQ steering are not used (the paper omits isolcpus and interrupt steering for all stacks), while Machnet dedicates a polling core. Against eRPC (a known-list project, not a category baseline) Machnet is slower: its median and p99 are within 10% of eRPC and p99.9 within 23%, and its 27 us median is 2 us higher. gRPC was not measured; the paper only asserts that libraries on top of Linux TCP such as gRPC would be slower. Only one Azure region was used, and the paper says cross-cloud numbers are not comparable. The paper's Raft text says '37% lower median p99', and Fig. 8 shows p99 625 vs 1000 us. On the repo side, the benchmark apps in the tree are src/apps/msg_gen, src/apps/rocksdb_server (not in the paper) and bindings/go/msg_gen; the FASTER server and Raft port are not in the tree, and the Linux side used sockperf. The README headline (750K 1KB RPCs/s at 61 us P99.9) has no baseline.

It is not A because the benchmark code exists only as partial modification snippets inside the doc (the rest_rpc multi-thread client_thread and its 'high-efficiency mode' are not shown, and there is no runnable bench file), explicit flags are not listed, and the comparison is against brpc, not gRPC.
verification.notes: The record's claimed_speedup had no numbers, so numbers_found_on_page is null. The README quote was checked word for word on master, and the rest_rpc-vs-brpc numbers above come from the cpp11-branch doc. If the orchestrator insists on gRPC as the baseline, the tier against gRPC itself stays D. Master's last commit is 2026-06-23; the record's 2026-09-08 came from the feature branch feat/client-seq-multiplexing. Status is still active; MIT license, not a fork, not archived, 2014 stars.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: "far exceeds gRPC" (README: 'rest_rpc是目前最快的rpc库，具体和grpc和brpc做了性能对比测试，rest_rpc性能是最高的，远超grpc') — no quantified figure given
corrected_fields.workload: Unspecified RPC echo/call workload; README claims a head-to-head performance comparison against gRPC and brpc was done, but no results table, numbers, or methodology are published
corrected_fields.caveats: README asserts it was benchmarked against gRPC and brpc and is much faster, and links to tests/bench.cpp, but that file only contains rest_rpc's own unthrottled echo loop (no gRPC/brpc code, no output numbers, no hardware/compiler info) — the comparative claim is unverifiable from anything in the repo. Counted as this run's single allowed Tier-D entry given >1k stars.
